description: We are a team of Year 11 students from Bangkok Patana School, Thailand, passionate about space exploration, engineering, technology, and innovation. Our skills include scientific research, programming, game development, and creative design. We enjoy combining science with interactive learning to make complex concepts engaging and accessible. We welcome teammates with skills in coding, UI/UX design, animation, or scientific research, as well as anyone who is creative and eager to learn!
summary:
Unfortunately, space-themed educational content aimed at younger students is often oversimplified and surface-level. Our project addresses this by creating an interactive learning experience that introduces students to the complex challenges of successfully managing a lunar outpost while remaining captivating and fun.

Players become mission commanders, making strategic decisions about food production, life support, oxygen supply, energy consumption, and astronaut safety. To ensure scientific accuracy, we based the game's facts and mechanics on six NASA sources, including the Artemis Base Camp concept, lunar radiation research, and Moon Base plan.

Through an interactive pixel-art lunar base, players can operate greenhouses and life-support systems, strengthen radiation shielding, and conduct scientific expeditions. They can also choose different lunar environments and solar conditions, each presenting unique challenges. Hands-on mini-games and unlockable upgrades make the experience engaging while demonstrating realistic engineering trade-offs: growing food consumes power, exploration increases radiation exposure, and solar storms force difficult decisions between safety and discovery.

Overall, our project makes space exploration accessible and engaging while encouraging critical thinking, problem-solving, and awareness of sustainable resource management.
details:
Project Overview:

Lunar Outpost is an interactive educational simulation in which players take on the role of a lone astronaut maintaining a lunar outpost at the Moon’s south pole for 12 days. Each day, players have three units of crew time to spend on five tasks: making air, growing food, piling moon dirt over the habitat for radiation shielding, taking science walks, and calling Earth for a space-weather forecast. Every task uses power, which is limited, so no choice is free. Players must also plan for lunar night, which arrives every fourth day with no sunlight, and for solar storms that can strike with little warning.

The game teaches engineering trade-offs by showing how one decision affects several systems. A science walk earns progress toward the mission goal but adds radiation dose, especially during a storm. Growing food drains power that the air plant also needs, and running out of power causes extra air loss overnight. Players can choose solar maximum or solar minimum, and a sunny ridge or an icy crater rim, each with different strengths and risks. Short mini-games make every task hands-on, and Tech Parts earned each mission can be spent on upgrades such as a rover or a stronger radiation shelter.

A mission fails if air or food reaches zero or radiation dose reaches 100. To succeed, players must survive all 12 days and complete at least 5 science walks. By building its facts and mechanics from six NASA sources, the game makes complex space exploration concepts accessible and engaging for children ages 7 to 12.

How does it Function?

This simulator focuses on five interconnected systems:

  1. Power management: You balance energy generation, storage, and consumption to maintain essential operations
  2. Radiation protection: You need to manage the astronauts' exposure to solar radiation and cosmic rays through shielding and safety decisions.
  3. Food and life support: By allocating food, water, and oxygen, you end up sustaining the crew for long missions on the Moon
  4. Infrastructure and resource efficiency: Comparing technologies and managing the resources needed to operate the outpost
  5. Mission challenges: Players respond to environmental hazards such as Solar storms and Lunar nights, as well as equipment failures.

Overall, players must consider the consequences of their choices and balance survival, efficiency, and scientific exploration.

Tools and Technologies

We developed Lunar Outpost using AI-assisted tools, software development resources, and NASA scientific research.

Claude AI and Chat GPT was used to extract and analyze scientific information from NASA publications and datasets. Claude AI also assisted with creating the game’s audio, elements and graphics.

GitHub was used to develop and organize the game’s foundational code and integrate the collected scientific information into the game.

Creativity and Innovation

Lunar Outpost transforms complex aerospace engineering concepts and survival logistics into a captivating and fun learning experience. Rather than simply presenting scientific facts, the game encourages players to apply knowledge through decision-making and problem-solving.

Its key innovation is connecting multiple engineering systems so that every choice involves a trade-off. Players learn that maintaining a space settlement requires balancing safety, sustainability, and limited resources rather than maximizing a single factor.

The combination of NASA research, simplified mathematical models, and child-friendly game design makes the project both educational and engaging.

Benefits, Impact, and Design Considerations

Lunar Outpost aims to inspire younger students to explore STEM subjects, particularly aerospace engineering, mathematics, and environmental science.

Through gameplay, users can develop:

  • Critical thinking: Evaluating the consequences of different decisions.
  • Problem-solving: Responding to unexpected challenges and resource shortages.
  • Scientific understanding: Learning how radiation, life-support systems, and resource limitations affect space exploration.
  • Sustainability awareness: Understanding the importance of recycling, efficiency, and responsible resource management.

The game is designed around clear visuals, accessible explanations, and age-appropriate challenges to make scientific concepts understandable without requiring advanced technical knowledge.

Ultimately, Junior Outpost demonstrates that successful space exploration depends on careful planning, engineering innovation, and balancing competing priorities.

AI use disclosure (Sanath)

Project: Moon Base Trade-Offs (lunar outpost STEM game)
Repository: hudsonruthling/moonbase-game
Game file: index.html
Purpose: Record AI assistance and human contributions transparently. This is a project disclosure, not legal advice or a claim that the project meets every event rule.

AI tools used

The project has used more than one AI assistant at different stages:

  1. Claude (Anthropic), web chat. We were using Claude Haiku 5.5 in one conversation to generate the starting version of the pixel-art game. We also supplied the challenge and NASA research context and requested a top-down, Terraria-style lunar base game for ages 7–12 with resources, shielding, power, and storms. We asked for keyboard and touch movement, a more detailed outdoor map with collisions, and an interior habitat with bunks, communications, rooms, and a sleep function. Claude generated the single-file HTML/CSS/JavaScript game and the associated “Did you know?” facts and source attribution from the supplied research brief.
  2. GitHub Copilot / OpenAI assistant in this repository conversation. An earlier prototype was drafted before the we switched to Claude. After we supplied the Claude-generated game source in chat, the assistant replaced the repository’s index.html with that source and has assisted with repository documentation. The earlier prototype was superseded and is no longer the current game.
